title: The two textures
teaches: What a cloud is made of, and why unstable air builds heaps while stable air forms flat sheets

parts.title: What a cloud is made of

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: A cloud is liquid water droplets (or ice), not water vapour.
Water vapour condenses into droplets when air cools to its **dew point**. The more vapour in the air, the higher its dew point.
Air cools when it rises: there is less air above pressing down, so it expands, and expanding air cools, by about 10 °C per kilometre.
So most clouds mark places where air is rising.
Air warmer than its surroundings is lighter, so it rises; cooler air sinks.

In **unstable** air a rising bubble stays warmer than the air around it and keeps going, building heaps: **cumulus**. In **stable** air it is pushed back, so cloud forms only when a whole layer is lifted or chilled: flat **stratus**.

blocks.text: Think of a boiling kettle. The white plume over the spout is not water vapour. Water vapour is water as a gas, made of individual molecules flying about on their own among the nitrogen and oxygen molecules of the air, and it is completely invisible. If you look closely at a boiling kettle, there is a clear gap right at the spout where the steam is still vapour. The white plume begins a finger’s width further out, where the vapour cools and its molecules clump together into microscopic liquid droplets. Individual gas molecules let light pass straight through, whereas liquid droplets are large enough to scatter light in every direction. Billions of droplets scattering sunlight in all directions look white.

A cloud is the same thing on a much larger scale. It is not water vapour, but tiny droplets of liquid water (or, very high up, tiny ice crystals) suspended in the air. So asking “why is there a cloud here?” is really asking “why did invisible vapour condense into liquid droplets here, and not over there?”

Water molecules in the air are constantly bumping into one another, and they are slightly sticky. Because each molecule is a little positive at one end and negative at the other, they tug on each other when they pass close by. Now and then a few stick together to start a droplet, but in warm air the molecules are jiggling so fast that they quickly shake themselves free again. The colder the air, the slower its molecules move, and the more likely they are to stay stuck once they collide. At the same time, the more water molecules you pack into a cubic metre of air, the more often they run into one another. At any temperature, there is a limit to how crowded the vapour can be before molecules stick together faster than they shake apart. Put in more vapour than that limit, and the excess condenses into liquid droplets. Warm air has a high limit: a cubic metre of air at 30 °C can keep about 30 grams of water as vapour, or roughly two spoonfuls. At 0 °C, that limit drops below 5 grams.

blocks.caption: The same water molecules in warm air and in cold air.

blocks.text: People often say that warm air “holds” more water, as if the air were a sponge. In fact, the nitrogen and oxygen aren’t holding anything. The water molecules simply share the air’s temperature, and it is that temperature, together with how crowded the vapour is, that determines whether the molecules stay loose as gas or clump into liquid. When people say air has “room for” a certain amount of water, they just mean that limit before condensation begins.

Now take some air with a fixed amount of water vapour in it and cool it down. At first nothing visible happens, because the vapour has not reached its limit yet. Keep cooling the air, and that limit shrinks until it equals the amount of water vapour actually present. That temperature is the air’s **dew point**. Cool the air below its dew point and the excess vapour condenses into droplets. It takes its name from morning dew on grass, where the cold blades chill the thin layer of air touching them below its dew point.

blocks.caption: A sealed jar of air with some water vapour in it. The violet curve is how much vapour there is room for at each temperature.
blocks.task: Cool the jar until it fogs.

blocks.text: Move the water slider in the jar and notice how the dew point behaves. First, the dew point depends only on how crowded the vapour is (how many grams of water vapour are in each cubic metre), not on how warm the air happens to be right now. If you add water vapour, the dew point goes up because the molecules are more crowded and need less cooling before they start sticking together. That makes the dew point a direct measure of how humid the air is. A dew point of 20 °C feels muggy, while a dew point of 0 °C feels crisp and dry.
Second, you don’t have to add any water to air to make a cloud. You only have to cool the air down to its dew point.

The atmosphere has a few ways of cooling air, but by far the most common is lifting it. To see why lifting cools air down, follow a single blob of air on its way up. In meteorology, a blob like this is called a **parcel**.

Of course, a parcel has no skin around it, and at its edges it is always mixing with the surrounding air. Even so, air genuinely moves in distinct blobs. A bubble of warm air rising off a sunny field can be a few hundred metres across and hold together for many minutes; hawks and glider pilots find these bubbles and circle inside them to climb. Because a blob that size mixes only around its outer edges, its core carries its own temperature and moisture upward. Treating a rising bubble as a self-contained parcel is a simplification, like a physicist’s frictionless ball, but it captures the essential physics.

Air near the ground is compressed by the weight of all the air piled above it, which comes to about ten tonnes on every square metre. We don’t feel crushed because the air and fluids inside our bodies push outward just as hard as the atmosphere pushes in. If you climb one kilometre, you leave about a tenth of the atmosphere below you, so there is a tenth less weight on top and the surrounding pressure is a tenth weaker. When a parcel of air rises into that lower pressure, the air inside it is still pushing outward at the higher pressure from below, so the parcel expands until its internal pressure drops to match the air outside.

When air expands, it cools. You have probably felt the opposite effect when pumping up a bicycle tyre, where compressing the air makes the pump warm. You can see expansion cooling directly if you pop open a cold bottle of fizzy drink: as the pressure drops, the gas in the neck expands, cools past its dew point, and forms a brief wisp of fog. Temperature is simply a measure of how fast molecules are jostling around. As a rising parcel expands, its molecules spend energy pushing the surrounding air out of the way, so they come away moving a little more slowly. Nothing cold has touched the parcel; it cools because its own molecules did the work of expanding.

blocks.caption: A parcel of air rising from the ground. Nothing is added or taken away; it just spreads out.

blocks.text: As long as no cloud has formed yet, a rising parcel cools at a steady rate of about 10 °C for every kilometre it climbs (9.8 °C, to be exact). This rate isn’t a rough average across different days. It follows directly from how hard gravity pulls on the atmosphere and how much heat energy air stores, so it is the same every day.

The parcel’s dew point also drops as it climbs, but much more slowly, at about 2 °C per kilometre. The parcel hasn’t lost any water, yet as it expands, the same water vapour is spread across a larger volume, leaving fewer grams of vapour in each cubic metre. Less crowded vapour has a lower dew point, just like sliding the water control down a little in the jar figure.

In a [[rising parcel|parcel]], two temperatures are converging: its actual temperature falls by about 10 °C per kilometre, while its [[dew point|dew]] falls by about 2 °C per kilometre. The gap between them closes by about 8 °C for every kilometre the parcel climbs.

blocks.caption: A parcel of air at ground level, 24 °C with a dew point of 12 °C.
blocks.task: Lift the air until it turns to cloud.

blocks.text: Where the two lines meet, the parcel has cooled to its dew point. Its vapour condenses into droplets, and the parcel becomes cloud. That height is the **cloud base**, and you can work it out directly from the ground readings. Because the gap closes by 8 °C every kilometre, each degree of gap at the ground takes 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 metres of lift to close. At the ground this morning, the gap is 24 − 12 = 12 °C, which puts the cloud base at about 12 × 125 = 1,500 metres above the ground.

You can see this relationship all summer. On a muggy day, the dew point starts out close to the air temperature, so rising air reaches condensation quickly and clouds form low. On a dry day, the gap is wide and cloud bases sit high. Try moving the dew point slider to see how the cloud base shifts.

In the atmosphere, water vapour needs a surface to condense onto. A cluster of just a few water molecules is so tiny and tightly curved that molecules escape from its surface far more easily than new ones stick, so it breaks apart before it can grow. Specks of dust, smoke, or sea salt give water molecules a larger surface to gather on, and every lungful of outdoor air contains millions of such specks. The resulting cloud droplets are tiny, about a hundredth of a millimetre across. Because of air resistance, droplets that small fall at less than a centimetre per second, slow enough for the slightest upward breeze to keep them aloft.

Most clouds mark places where air has risen and cooled below its dew point. (A few, such as fog, form when air cools right where it sits near the ground.) What makes one cloud look so different from another is mostly *how* the air rose: in separate buoyant bubbles, or all together as a wide layer.

Why does air sometimes rise in isolated bubbles and other times stay in a flat layer? Suppose you give a parcel of air a small push upward. On some days, that parcel will keep rising on its own. On other days, it will sink right back down to where it started. Which way the atmosphere behaves on a given day determines almost everything about the clouds that form.

Air rises on its own for the same reason a hot-air balloon does. A parcel of warm air is under the same pressure as the air immediately around it. Because its molecules are moving faster, however, it takes fewer molecules per cubic metre to push outward and match that surrounding pressure. Having fewer molecules in each cubic metre makes the warm parcel less dense than the cooler air around it, so the heavier surrounding air slides underneath and buoys it upward.

While a rising dry parcel always cools at about 10 °C per kilometre, the [[air around it|env]] also changes temperature with height, and that surrounding profile varies from day to day. Averaged over the whole earth and year, the atmosphere gets colder by about 6.5 °C per kilometre of altitude. On a hot afternoon when strong sunshine bakes the ground, the lowest kilometre or two can get colder with height by more than 10 °C per kilometre. On a clear morning after the ground has cooled all night, the temperature may drop much more slowly with height, or even get warmer as you go up. A warm layer sitting on top of cooler air is called an **inversion**. You can often see an inversion when smoke or valley haze rises to a certain height and spreads out flat, unable to climb through the warm layer above.

To see what happens to a nudged parcel, compare the two cooling rates. Push a parcel up a few hundred metres, and it cools at 10 °C per kilometre on the way. If the surrounding air gets colder with height *faster* than that, say at 12 °C per kilometre, the parcel arrives at its new altitude warmer and less dense than its new neighbours. Because it is warmer and lighter, it keeps rising on its own, and the higher it climbs, the greater its temperature lead becomes. Meteorologists call this **unstable** air.

If instead the surrounding air gets colder with height *more slowly* than 10 °C per kilometre, say at 5 °C per kilometre, the nudged parcel arrives colder and denser than its new neighbours. Being heavier than the air around it, it sinks back down to where it started. That air is **stable**. Notice that stable and unstable describe the temperature profile of the surrounding sky on that day, which governs what happens to any parcel that gets nudged.

blocks.caption: Two days, two skies. Each bubble is nudged up one kilometre and cools 10 °C; what decides its fate is the air around it.

blocks.text: A ball on a landscape behaves the same way. At the bottom of a valley, push the ball and it rolls back to where it started, which is stable. Balanced on a hilltop, push the ball and it rolls away and keeps going, which is unstable. In the figure, compare the two temperatures beside the bubble as it moves.

blocks.caption: A bubble of air nudged upward. Its own temperature is orange; the air around it is violet.
blocks.task: Nudge the bubble once in stable air and once in unstable air.

blocks.text: Those two behaviours give the sky its two basic textures. In unstable air, warm bubbles shoot up on their own wherever heated ground gives them a start, and each bubble builds its own cloud, forming **heaps**. In stable air, nothing climbs by itself. Air turns to cloud only if something cools a whole layer from outside, such as wind pushing air steadily up a mountain slope or cold ground chilling the air resting on it. When a wide layer is cooled gently all together, it forms a flat **sheet**.

Nearly every cloud in the low sky is a heap, a sheet, or a combination of the two, such as heaps that flatten out against a stable layer into a lumpy sheet. Later lessons cover those combinations, along with the high, icy wisps that form near the top of the troposphere. First, let’s look closely at pure heaps and pure sheets.

Sunlight passes through clear air almost without warming it. The ground absorbs the sunlight instead, and the warm ground heats the air touching it. Different surfaces warm up at different rates: dark rock, bare fields, and roofs get hot quickly, while a lake or a damp forest spends much of the sun’s energy evaporating water and stays cooler.

Over a hot patch of ground, the air warms, becomes less dense than the cooler air around it, and eventually breaks free to rise as a bubble called a **thermal**. A thermal behaves just like the parcel we followed earlier, cooling at 10 °C per kilometre as it expands and closing the gap to its dew point. Where temperature and dew point meet, water vapour condenses into droplets and the top of the thermal becomes visible as a heap of cloud: a **cumulus**.

blocks.caption: A sunny morning over farm country. Thermals rise from the warmest ground.
blocks.task: Bring the sun up until two clouds have formed.

blocks.text: In the figure, notice that every heap starts at the same height, giving cumulus clouds **flat bases** all at one level. You might expect a bubble rising off the hottest rock to start out much warmer and reach its dew point much higher up. In practice, by mid-morning the rising thermals have stirred the lowest kilometre of the sky so thoroughly that the air across the valley has nearly uniform temperature and moisture. A bubble breaks away as soon as it is a degree or so warmer than its surroundings, which changes its condensation height by a hundred metres at most. Seen from across the valley, the cloud bases line up along a flat level.

Moving the **moisture** slider shifts that level up or down. Humid air starts with a small gap between temperature and dew point, so its cloud bases are low; dry air starts with a wide gap, so its bases are high. Because a thermal only keeps rising while it remains warmer than the air around it, on very dry days the rising bubbles lose their temperature lead and stop climbing before they ever reach their dew point. The thermals then stay completely invisible, leaving a blue, cloudless sky that is still bumpy for gliders.

Why doesn’t a rising bubble stop once it reaches the cloud base? When water evaporates, it absorbs heat energy, which is why sweat cools your skin as it dries. When water vapour condenses back into liquid droplets inside a cloud, it releases that stored heat back into the surrounding air. That heat warms the cloudy parcel from within, so above the cloud base the rising air cools by only about 5 °C per kilometre instead of 10 °C. Whether the parcel keeps rising still depends on comparing its cooling rate with the air around it. Often the surrounding air a kilometre or two up gets colder by 6 or 7 °C per kilometre. A dry thermal cooling at 10 °C per kilometre would quickly become colder than that surrounding air and stop rising. A cloudy thermal cooling at 5 °C per kilometre stays warmer than its surroundings, so its buoyancy increases and it keeps billowing upward in bright, cauliflower-like towers.

Between the cumulus clouds, the sky stays clear. Every bit of air that rises in a thermal must be replaced by air sinking somewhere else. As the air between the thermals sinks into higher pressure, it is compressed and warms by 10 °C per kilometre, moving its temperature further above its dew point so no cloud can form.

blocks.caption: A fair-weather cumulus, and the air moving around it.

blocks.text: Small cumulus scattered across a blue sky are the best weather there is, and they are called fair-weather cumulus. They appear with the morning sun and fade around sunset, when the ground stops heating the air and the thermals shut down.
To form a flat blanket of cloud instead of isolated heaps, a broad layer of stable air has to be cooled gently all together, often without any lifting at all.

Every warm object radiates infrared light, which our eyes cannot see but which carries heat energy away. During the day, the sun pours more energy into the ground than the ground radiates upward. At night no sunlight comes in, and under a clear sky the ground’s infrared radiation escapes straight out to space. As the ground cools, the air resting on it loses heat to the cold surface by contact, the way your hand cools on a cold windowpane. Contact alone chills only the bottom few centimetres, but gentle stirring in the night air, along with the air’s own infrared radiation, spreads the chill upward through the lowest few tens of metres. Clouds radiate infrared heat back down toward the ground as well, which is why a cloudy night stays mild while a clear night turns cold.

blocks.caption: What the ground gains and loses, by day and by night.

blocks.text: Cooling from below leaves the coldest, densest air at the bottom with warmer air above it. That creates an inversion, which is the most stable arrangement possible because the heaviest air is already as low as it can go. Nothing bubbles upward; the chilled layer simply deepens slowly through the night. Unlike a rising parcel, this surface air stays at the same pressure and does not expand, so its water vapour is not spread any thinner and its dew point stays constant while its temperature drops toward it.

blocks.caption: A night in a valley.
blocks.task: Find a night that ends in fog by dawn.

blocks.text: A cloud that forms on the ground is **fog**. In the figure, the cooling slows down later in the night because colder ground radiates less heat. Watch what the wind slider does as well. A light breeze stirs only the bottom few dozen metres of chilled air, spreading the cold upward so the fog grows deeper. A strong wind stirs a much deeper layer, mixing warmer air down from above the inversion so the air near the ground never gets cold enough for fog to form.

Fog and **stratus** are the exact same cloud; the name only indicates whether the cloud base touches the ground. When a morning breeze or the first warmth of the sun evaporates the bottom of a fog bank, the layer left hanging above is stratus: a flat, uniform sheet with no distinct features, often low enough to hide the hilltops. Stratus also forms during the day or night whenever warm, moist air drifts across cold ground or cold sea water and gets chilled from below. In either case, stable air is cooled gently as a wide layer, forming an unbroken sheet.

blocks.caption: The same layer of cloud, seen from the valley floor.

blocks.text: Seen from below, stratus looks grey. It is made of the same water droplets as a white cumulus cloud, but because a stratus layer covers the sky, you see only its shaded underside while its sunlit top faces away from you. The flat base of a cumulus cloud looks grey for the same reason; a cumulus looks bright white only where you can see sunlight hitting its sides and rounded top. If you fly above a stratus deck, its upper surface is dazzling white.

A thick layer of stratus can bring drizzle. The tiny droplets inside bump into one another as they drift, and now and then two merge. After an hour or so in a thick layer, enough merging takes place to produce drops a few tenths of a millimetre across. Those larger drops fall at one or two metres per second, far faster than any gentle air current in a quiet, stable layer can hold up, so they sink out of the cloud as drizzle.

Stratus is more of a nuisance than a danger. It brings drizzle at worst, and it usually burns off by late morning. Sunlight filters through the layer and warms the ground, the ground warms the air from below, and once the air’s temperature climbs back above its dew point, the droplets evaporate back into vapour.
The photos below are real skies. Name each one: cumulus heaps or a stratus blanket.
**Cumulus**: separate heaps with flat bases, bright tops, and blue sky between them. **Stratus**: a flat, uniform grey layer with no gaps, often hiding the hills.

blocks.caption: The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: Small, flat-bottomed heaps popped up mid-morning and have stayed small all day, drifting across a blue sky. Is it safe to leave cut hay out to dry?
options: Yes: fair-weather cumulus, and they will fade by evening
No: heaps like these mean rain by evening
items.why: Small cumulus that stay small are thermals topping out under stable air. They come with the morning sun and fade when the ground stops heating the air: fair weather.

items.question: After a clear, still, damp night, a grey blanket lies on the ground at dawn and hides the hilltops. When can a plane expect to take off?
options: Mid to late morning, once the sun has burned it off
Right away: fog is thinnest at dawn
Not today: a blanket like this means a storm
items.why: On a clear, still night the ground cools the air above it below its dew point. After sunrise the sun warms the ground, the ground warms the air, and once the air is warmer than its dew point again the fog evaporates, usually by mid to late morning.

learned: A cloud is made of liquid droplets (or ice crystals), not water vapour. Air forms a cloud when it cools to its dew point, and the more water vapour a cubic metre of air contains, the higher its dew point.
Rising air expands and cools by about 10 °C per kilometre, while its dew point falls by about 2 °C per kilometre, closing the gap between them by 8 °C per kilometre.
The cloud base sits about 125 m above the ground for each degree Celsius between the surface temperature and the dew point, forming low on humid days and high on dry ones.

Air is unstable when the surrounding atmosphere gets colder with height faster than a rising bubble cools (10 °C per kilometre in clear air, or about 5 °C per kilometre inside a cloud). A nudged bubble keeps rising on its own, building cumulus heaps with flat bases and bright tops.
In stable air, a nudged bubble becomes colder than its surroundings and sinks back down. It forms cloud only when a whole layer is lifted or chilled together, creating stratus or ground fog.
next: Next lesson covers the rest of the low sky, from lumpy sheets that bring dry weather to thick grey layers that bring steady rain.

what-is-a-cloud.title: What a cloud is
what-is-a-cloud.text: A cloud consists of tiny liquid droplets (or ice crystals), not water vapour. Air turns to cloud when cooled to its dew point, the temperature below which excess water vapour condenses into liquid; the more humid the air, the higher its dew point. Because rising dry air expands and cools by about 10 °C per kilometre while its dew point falls by about 2 °C per kilometre, the cloud base forms about 125 m up for each degree Celsius between the temperature and dew point at the ground.

stability.title: Stable and unstable air
stability.text: A rising dry parcel cools at 10 °C per kilometre. If the surrounding air gets colder with height faster than that, a lifted parcel ends up warmer than its neighbours and keeps rising on its own; this is unstable air, which builds heaps. If the surrounding air cools more slowly with height, or warms with height in an inversion, a lifted parcel ends up colder than its neighbours and sinks back down; this is stable air, which turns to cloud only when a whole layer is cooled together into flat sheets.

cumulus.title: Cumulus
cumulus.text: Separate heaps of cloud with flat bases and bright, rounded tops, built by rising thermals on sunny days. Small ones indicate fair weather, while towers still growing tall at midday can bring afternoon showers.

stratus.title: Stratus
stratus.text: A flat, uniform grey layer low enough to hide the hills, essentially fog whose base is off the ground. It forms by gentle cooling of stable air, either overnight or while drifting over cold ground or water. It brings light drizzle at most and often burns off by midday.
